title: Beyond the Data
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Written at the start of an academic year, this piece assembles the evidence that pupil motivation in English secondary schools is in crisis and then uses Polyn and Woodman's review to argue that the psychological conditions of learning deserve the attention usually given to measurable outputs. The data is stark: UCL research placing English secondary pupils among the least emotionally engaged internationally, the Mind the Engagement Gap report finding one in four children disengaging in their first secondary year with enjoyment falling from about 6.0 in Year 6 to 3.2 by Year 8, and the IPPR's description of a crisis of lost learning. Hughes then walks the constructs the review identifies, motivation, self-regulation, self-efficacy, mindset, emotion regulation and goal orientation, insisting these are not form-time extras but central to how pupils learn. Each gets a classroom translation: autonomy, competence and belonging rather than reward systems; modelled planning and reflection pauses for self-regulation; scaffolding and strategy feedback rather than growth-mindset exhortation. The emotion section carries the sharpest mechanism, that anxiety degrades working memory, and the closing section contrasts performance goals with mastery goals.
points: The engagement data is specific enough to act on, with enjoyment falling from about 6.0 in Year 6 to 3.2 by Year 8 and one in four pupils disengaging in their first secondary year.
The six psychological constructs are positioned as central to learning rather than as pastoral extras confined to PSHE or form time.
The mindset caveat is important: interventions only work alongside the right classroom conditions, so telling pupils they can grow without showing them how achieves nothing.
The emotion-regulation mechanism is the most directly usable, since anxiety and embarrassment degrade working memory and so block both encoding and retrieval.
The performance-versus-mastery contrast connects grading and feedback practice to anxiety and surface learning, with concrete alternatives for shifting pupils toward mastery.
quotes: There is growing evidence that pupil motivation is at crisis point in English secondary schools, especially among early adolescents.
Enjoyment plummets from around 6.0 in Year 6 to just 3.2 by Year 8.
These are not ‘nice to haves’ or side conversations for form time, or even shoe-horned just into PSHE, they sit at the heart of how students learn, think and behave.

Yet the review warns that well-intentioned systems built around rewards, praise or sanctions can sometimes undermine motivation, particularly if pupils begin to associate success with external approval alone.
In short, telling pupils they can grow isn’t enough, we have to show them how, through consistent practice, scaffolding and feedback that emphasises progress and strategy.
In other words, if a pupil is feeling anxious, embarrassed or unsafe, their brain is less able to process new information or retrieve prior knowledge.
Emotional safety isn’t about lowering expectations. It’s about removing unnecessary barriers to learning so that all pupils have the best chance to succeed.
